10037935:
Testimony in Support of LD 327: An Act to Provide Additional Funding to Support In-home Personal Support Services for Qualified Senior Citizens
March 12, 2025
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and members of the Committee on Health and Human Services:
My name is Bev Uhlenhake, I am a Government Affairs Consultant at Pierce Atwood, and I am presenting the following testimony in Support of LD 327 on behalf of the Maine Association of Personal Care Agencies, a group of businesses whose work assists primarily older adults and people with disabilities in Maine to remain in their homes longer, maintain relationships with family and neighbors, and generally live healthier, happier lives. While not all PCAs are funded by MaineCare, those that are are generally funded in part through Section 19.
As you know, personal support services refer to the assistance with daily living activities offered to older adults and people with disabilities. These services include a wide range of activities from helping with basic personal hygiene and making food to ensuring cleanliness in the home and providing a social outlet for those who feel isolated. The work of personal care agencies might seem menial, but their presence in the homes of older Mainers and those with disabilities can save lives. It is often the direct support workers who are the first to notice the early signs of the onset of illness or deterioration of abilities. They are also the ones who find people who have fallen or have otherwise become incapacitated. Their work is incredibly vital to older Mainers and people with disabilities.
The presence of personal support services is also important to our economy. As noted in the Joint Resolution to Support Family Caregivers in Maine that was passed on February 25th, "Maine is missing out on over $1,000,000,000 per year in additional economic activity as a result of family caregivers dropping out of the labor force due to care challenges." With additional funding for personal support services, more Mainers could reenter the workforce and add to our economy in very real ways.
Supporting additional funding for personal support services in Maine is both a moral obligation to older adults and people with disabilities in Maine, but it also makes good financial sense. I urge you support LD 327.
Thank you for your consideration in this matter.
Respectfully submitted,
Beverly B. Uhlenhake On behalf of Maine Association of Personal Care Agencies

Testimony of Rep. Bill Bridgeo introducing
LD 327, An Act to Provide Additional Funding to Support In-home Personal
Support Services for Qualified Senior Citizens Before the Health and Human Services Committee
Good afternoon, Sen. Ingwersen, Rep. Meyer and esteemed members of the Health and Human Services
Committee. My name is Bill Bridgeo, and I represent House District 60, which is part of the great City of Augusta. I am here today to present LD 327, An Act to Provide Additional Funding to Support In-home
Personal Support Services for Qualified Senior Citizens.
Although, technically speaking, I brought this bill forward at the request of a friend, retired Maine journalist John
Hale (who will follow me as a proponent of the bill), I should state clearly that I believe that this bill addresses a
significant problem in our state and that is the shortfall in funding to support in-home support services for Maine's
senior population.
I'm certainly no expert in the various programs that exist in Maine to help seniors -- those qualifying for
MaineCare and others -- but I know enough about the situation to appreciate that there is more need out there than
there is funding, and that dollars spent keeping seniors from unnecessarily long hospital stays or from nursing
home institutionalization is a prudent investment of scarce state resources -- not to mention the humane thing to
do.
I l1ave learned from helpful conversations with DHHS leadership that there are several existing programs in place.
Two are directed to seniors qualifying for MaineCare (Sections 19 and 96 of the department's relevant
regulations) and one for seniors whose assets put them above MaineCare thresholds but who, as a practical matter, would struggle to aflord in-home care (Section 63 of the regs).
LD 327, as drafted, would direct $1 million a year to the MaineCare-eligible program. However, it appears that
there is a lack of data about the true extent of the need as waiting lists are not currently maintained by the
department.
For that reason, I'm in hopes the bill can be amended to direct the $1 million in funding to the State Section 63 program and to require DI-ll-IS to establish such lists (My understanding is that Representative Cluchey has a
resolve -- LD 977 -- that would charge the Maine Health Data Organization with doing just that).
I appreciate that we are in difficult budgetary times, but I really do believe that money invested in these in-home programs will, in the long run, be a net gain for the state -- and for the Mainers who are thus able to remain in their
homes.
Thank you for your attention to this important issue. I'm happy to answer questions to the extent I can.
10036898:
Testimony of Brenda Peluso on Behalf of Maine's Essential Care & Support Workforce Partnership
Submitted on March 12, 2025
Testimony in Support of LD 327: An Act to Provide Additional Funding to Support In-home Personal Support Services for Qualified Senior Citizens
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and members of the Committee on Health and Human Services:
My name is Brenda Peluso, and I am the coordinator for Maine's Essential Care & Support Workforce Partnership, a broad coalition of employers, workers, and concerned individuals working to increase access to quality direct care and support in Maine by changing the way we value workers and the work they do.
We believe LD 327 will produce a good return on investment. The Personal Support Services funded in this bill, allow older Mainers and people with disabilities to stay in their homes as long as possible - where they prefer to be - where they do best - and where their care costs the least. Additionally, they allow loved ones, their family caregivers, to remain in the workforce.
The following is an excerpt from the 2023 report1, commissioned by the Essential Care & Support Workforce and published by the Maine Center on Economic Policy:
 Our collective failure to adequately support direct care workers is keeping more than 8,000 people out of Maine's labor force.
 Maine is missing out on over $1 billion per year in additional economic activity as a result of people dropping out of the labor force due to direct care challenges.
 Undervaluing care work imposes significant public costs on our state, as low wages lead more workers to rely on public assistance programs, including MaineCare and Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). Meanwhile, the drop in labor force participation due to direct care responsibilities means fewer workers are contributing taxes. These combine to cost our state and federal budgets more than $70 million each year.
 Direct care workforce shortages place undue strains on Maine's health care system. In March 2023, Maine Medical Center had about 50 people under its care who were approved for discharge but could not find an alternative care setting; meanwhile, Northern Light Health noted that over a nearly six-month period, the cost of delayed discharges across the system's hospitals totaled $13.6 million and amounted to approximately $63,000 per person.
1 "The High Cost of Undervaluing Direct Care Work," MECEP, April 2023, https://essentialworkforce.org/2023/04/the-high-cost-of-undervaluing-direct-care-work-2/

Personal Support Services include a wide range of activities from helping with basic personal hygiene and making food to ensuring cleanliness in the home and providing a social outlet for those who feel isolated. While these services may seem inconsequential, they are critical to the health and well-being of so many of our family members, neighbors, and friends.
Sadly, there is a severe shortage in this workforce. For example, over 23,500 hours of approved home care for older adults go undelivered each week2 and this un-provided care results in the economic and human costs mentioned above.
Any investments we can make that grow this workforce are smart investments and I urge you to support LD 327.
Thank you for all your careful consideration of the priorities in front of you. Our partnership is committed to serving as a trusted resource on this critical workforce.

AARP Maine Testimony in support of LD 327 An Act to Provide Additional Funding to Support In-home Personal Support Services for Qualified Senior Citizens
Greetings Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and members of the Committee on Health and Human Services. My name is Bridget Quinn, Associate State Director of Advocacy and Outreach for AARP Maine.
AARP is the nation's largest nonprofit, nonpartisan organization dedicated to empowering Americans 50 and older to choose how they live as they age. On behalf of our nearly 200,000 members statewide, thank you for the opportunity to share testimony today. Today I am testifying in support of LD 327 and want to take a moment to share with the committee the importance of community care in Maine.
Time and time again AARP research nationally and in Maine have found that older adults want to age in their homes. A 2024 survey of Mainers 45+ conducted by AARP found that Most Maine adults age 45+ prefer to age in place with caregiver assistance. In fact, 82% would prefer to receive care at home with caregiver assistance when the basic tasks of life become more difficult. Further, 87% say it's extremely or very important to be able to stay in their own home as they get older. 1
For many of us to age in our communities comfortably we will need support. This is where the support for in-home personal support services is critical. A resource I'd like to share with committee members is AARP's Long-Term Services and Supports Scorecard. The Scorecard compares state LTSS systems across multiple dimensions of performance, reflecting the importance and interconnectedness each has on the overall LTSS system. The goal is to spark conversations, inspire investment, galvanize broad-based coalitions, and focus stakeholders' attention on the factors that most directly impact consumers and their families. So though some of the facts I share as Maine compares across states will sound drastic the intention is to think about how we can better support all Mainers.
The cost of private pay home care in Maine is nearly the costliest. Compared to other states we rank 49th. The annual cost of private pay home care is more than the median household
1 Bonner Cozad, Aisha, Kate Bridges, and Cassandra Cantave. AARP Vital Voices Research, 20222024. Washington, DC: AARP Research, September 2022. https://doi.org/10.26419/res.00524.000

income of those age 65+. 2 We must adequately fund MaineCare covered Home Care programs to protect those of a low income from having too potentially pay these high costs. Nationally Maine ranks 20th in supply of home health aides. There are approximately 22.8 home health aides for every 100 individuals in Maine who need one. At AARP Maine we are supportive of this legislation. We have concerns surrounding the needed funding for this bill. So we seek to offer opportunities for Maine to continue to explore that will hopefully alleviate the crunch on our long-term care system. This includes implementing Medicaid Presumptive Eligibility in Maine and seeking ways to increase enrollment and use of Medicaid's self-directed program. We hope to continue to work with the bill sponsor and this committee to come up with solutions to supporting those who want to age in place but need some help to do so. Thank you for the opportunity to provide testimony today, if you have further questions for me I can be contacted at bquinn@aarp.org or at 207-272-8563. Thank you, Bridget Quinn AARP Maine

10036725:
LD 327 - An Act to Provide Additional Funding to Support In-home Personal Support Services for Qualified Senior Citizens
Testimony of John Brautigam, Esq. for Legal Services for Maine Elders Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services
March 12, 2025
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services.
My name is John Brautigam, and I am here today on behalf of Legal Services for Maine Elders. LSE provides free legal help for Mainers aged 60 and older when their basic human needs are at stake.
Thank you for the opportunity to testify in support of LD 327 and increased funding for in-home personal support services for qualified beneficiaries.
As you are aware, in-home personal support services provide essential assistance to older adults who need help with daily activities such as bathing, dressing, meal preparation, medication management, and mobility. These services enable older Mainers to remain in their communities, maintain their independence, and avoid costly and often undesirable institutionalization in nursing homes.
Unfortunately, funding has not kept pace with the increasing demand for these services. Many lowincome seniors who qualify for assistance face long waiting lists, inadequate caregiver availability, and insufficient support hours to meet their needs. Without stable and adequate funding, folks are left struggling to manage alone or are forced into institutional care. Even the best assisted housing or nursing home facilities represent a downturn in the well-being of many of the individuals forced to leave their homes. They are also more expensive for taxpayers.
Expanding funding for in-home personal support services is not just a matter of compassion, it is sound fiscal policy. Studies consistently show that providing care in the home is significantly more cost-effective than nursing home placement1. The average annual cost of home care is a fraction of
1 The cost of an "Aging in Place" program was significantly less than nursing home care in one recent study. Marek KD, Stetzer F, Adams SJ, Popejoy LL, Rantz M. Aging in place versus nursing home care: comparison of costs to Medicare and Medicaid. Res Gerontol Nurs. 2012 Apr;5(2):123-9. doi: 10.3928/19404921-20110802-01. Epub 2011 Aug 17. PMID: 21846081.
LEGAL SERVICES FOR MAINE ELDERS, INC. 5 Wabon Street, Augusta, Maine 04333 (207) 621-0087 Fax (207) 621-0742
Offices in Augusta, Bangor, Lewiston, Biddeford and Presque Isle LSE Helpline 1-800-750-5353 (Voice/TTY) www.mainelse.org

March 12, 2025 Legal Services for Maine Elders - LD 327 Page 2
the cost of institutional care, and investing in these services now will reduce the financial burden on Medicaid and other state resources in the long term.
Increased funding would also help stabilize the workforce of home care aides, ensuring that caregivers receive fair wages and can continue providing these essential services. You know very well that workforce shortages are a growing crisis in the long-term care sector, and without action, our most vulnerable citizens will face even greater difficulties accessing the care they need.
I respectfully urge you to prioritize the needs of older Mainers by adding funds for in-home personal support services. Doing so will allow more seniors to age in place, maintain their independence, and receive the dignified care they deserve.
Thank you.

Statement of John Hale of North Monmouth on LD 327
To the Maine Legislature's Joint Committee on Health and Human Services
Greetings, Senate Chairman Ingersen, House Chairman Meyers and members of the
Health and Human Services Committee.
My name is John Hale. From 1986 to 1997, I was State House bureau chief for the
Bangor Daily News. It is good to be back at the State House, to see some old friends and see the many changes that have taken place.
Unfortunately, in retirement, I was hospitalized mostly at St. Mary's rehab center,
D'Youville Pavilion in Lewiston for ll weeks in 2018, the last year the Red Sox won the
World Series. And I was hospitalized again last year for 5 weeks after having my left knee
replaced, also at Central Maine Medical Center, after which I was housed at a rehab facility called Marshwood Rehabilitation Center in Lewiston. During these long hospital
stays, I observed a major gap in Maine's postsurgical home health care for seniors and that
is what this bill is intended correct.
One area that is completely lacking, but is very important is overnight care at home for seniors who live alone who return home after major surgeries, such as joint replacements which have become veiy common in Maine. MaineCare doesn't pay for this critical
benefit for the most part so patients are expected to pay for a nighttime companion and
caregiver out of their own pockets. The patient also is expected to find someone, a neighbor perhaps, who is willing to stay all night near the patient's sleeping area. I found it's very hard to find anybody who's willing to stay for even one night, much less the 2-3 weeks that we believe is necessary for a safe recovery.
Why is this nonexistent benefit so important? It's because the person returning home
from the hospital is weak and disoriented and prone to nighttime falls that can seriously
injure them or even end their life. According to recent research done for the Maine DHHS, Maine is now the No. 1 "grayest" state in the nation, with the highest percentage of people
age 65 and older. There are more than 300,000 seniors living in Maine and the study
estimates that well over 100,000 of them live alone. Just think of an older couple you may know in their 80s or 90s who have been happily married for 60 years or more. They have a

full, happy life until one of them falls and dies. Then the other previously independent partner languishes and either dies or goeslfrom living at home to living at an expensive nursing home.

Testimony in support:
LD 327, "An Act to Provide Additional Funding to Support In-home Personal Support Services
for Qualified Senior Citizens"
Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services
March 12th, 2025

Good afternoon, Senator lngwersen, Representative Meyer, and members of the committee on
Health and Human Services, my name is Laura Harper. I am a Senior Associate for Moose Ridge Associates. i am here today to present testimony on behalf of the Maine Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program.

The Ombudsman Program provides statewide advocacy for residents of nursing homes, assisted housing including residential care and assisted living and for recipients of home care
and adult day services. Additionally, the program serves patients waiting for discharge from the
hospital who encounter barriers in accessing the long-term services and supports they need.

This legislation provides ongoing funding for in-home personal support services provided to adults with disabilities under rule Chapter 101: MaineCare Benefits Manual, Chapter ll, Section
19, Home and Community Benefits for the Elderly and Adults with Disabilities. We support
funding for this critically needed home care program that allows thousands of Mainers to remain
at home.

As of December 2024, OADS reported that Section 19 has 3,005 participants. To qualify for Section 19 Home and Community Benefits Waiver (HCB), you must meet the eligibility criteria for nursing home level of care. Section 19 HCB gives those with the highest level of need that
otherwise would be institutionalized in a facility, the ability to remain at home. Access to nursing
home level of care at home has never been more critical, considering the increase in nursing home closures. Since 2021, there have been 16 nursing home closures, making it incredibly difficult for Mainers to find a nursing home opening in their own community.

Additionally, Section 19 HCB allows those living in institutions the opportunity to transition back
into the community. Known nationally as Money Follows the Person, Maine's Homeward Bound program helps seniors and adults with disabilities transition from nursing homes and hospitals

back to community-based care settings. Homeward Bound participants will receive support in accessing home and community-based services as well as services including specialized clinical assessments, independent living assistance, household start-up, enhanced care
coordination, technology services and more. Almost all participants transition into the
community by accessing the Section 19 HCB waiver.
lf Maine wants to support older adults and adults with disabilities to remain at home, Section 19
HCB funding should be the top priority.
Thank you for your time and consideration.

Re: LD 327 - An Act to Provide Additional Funding to Support In-home Personal Support Services for Qualified Senior Citizens

Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services:

I'm writing to provide information about LD 327, which would appropriate additional funds for MaineCare Section 19, the home and community-based waiver program for older adults and individuals with physical disabilities.

Currently, we have no wait list for Section 19. The program serves just over 3,000 individuals and continues to accept applications from qualified persons, who must meet MaineCare financial requirements and have functional needs that would otherwise qualify them for nursing home level of care.

While support for this critical program is certainly appreciated, additional funding would not have any impact on services, since we are able to continue serving all qualified applicants.

Please let me know if I can provide any additional information about Section 19.

Sincerely,

Paul Saucier, Director Office of Aging and Disability Services Maine Department of Health and Human Services
10036787:
Home Care & Hospice Alliance of Maine Testimony on LD 327 An Act to Provide Additional Funding to Support In-home Personal Support
Services for Qualified Senior Citizens
March 12, 2025
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and members of the Health & Human Services Committee:
My name is Sara Ratcliffe, and I serve as Executive Director of the Home Care and Hospice Alliance of Maine. The Alliance is submitting testimony in support of LD 327, An Act to Provide Additional Funding to Support In-home Personal Support Services for Qualified Senior Citizens.
The Home Care and Hospice Alliance of Maine is a network of home care, hospice, and personal care providers across our State delivering in-home care to older adults and disabled individuals of all ages, allowing them to stay in their homes and communities.
The Alliance would like to thank Rep. Bridgeo for submitting this bill to help address unmet needs for in-home services for older Mainers. Home care is a critical part of Maine's health care continuum. By caring for people at home, we keep them out of more costly settings like hospitals and nursing homes.
Older Mainers primarily receive in-home services through three programs - MaineCare Section 19, which is Home and Community Benefits for Elderly and Adults with Disabilities, MaineCare Section 96, which is Private Duty Nursing and Personal Care Services, and State-funded Program Section 63, which is In-Home and Community Support Services for Elderly and Other Adults. Sec. 63 serves adults who do not qualify for MaineCare.
Unfortunately, there are significant unmet needs in all three of these programs. I have attached to my testimony a table from a 2024 report to this committee: Efforts and Progress in Implementing the Recommendations of the Commission to Study Long-term Care Workforce Issues, pub. 2/2024 (PDF) - Third Annual Report Pursuant to PL 2021, c. 398, Section AAAA-7. As you can see from this table, 50% of the patients enrolled in Sec. 19 are not receiving the services for which they are eligible. That number jumps to 62% for patients in Sec. 96 and 71% for patients enrolled in Sec. 63. In some cases, people may be receiving fewer hours of service than what they qualify for. In other cases, people may be receiving zero hours of service.
According to data provided on the Office of Aging and Disability Services website, as of Dec. 2024, there were 969 individuals on the waitlist for Sec. 63 services. The department

does not keep waitlists for Sections 19 and 96, so it's difficult to determine how many people are going without services entirely.
The reasons for these unmet needs are multifaceted, but inadequate MaineCare reimbursement rates certainly play a large role for Sections 19 and 96. Providers in these programs are unable to attract and retain the workforce needed to meet service needs due to low reimbursement rates from MaineCare. For Section 63, the needs for service outpace the state appropriation provided for the program.
The department has been engaged in a rate determination process for Home and Community Based Services for much of the past year, and has said that the process will wrap up next month, however no funds were proposed in the Biennial Budget to fund rate increases for these sections of MaineCare.
We deeply appreciate Rep. Bridgeo's attempt to try to tackle this issue. Whether through rate increases for Sections 19 and 96, or through an increased appropriation for Section 63 - or better yet, both - this is a problem that needs to be fixed. We should be striving to ensure older Mainers can live at home and in their communities for as long as possible. Adequate home care services are a critical part of meeting that goal.
Thank you,
Sara Ratcliffe Executive Director Home Care & Hospice Alliance of Maine Sara@FrontlineCo.com
